_about: Real cooking tips and facts shown in the corner of a close-up while you cook (CookSession). 'topics' are facts by subject. 'recipes', by recipe id (data/recipes/<id>.tres): 'steps' are tips for one step (by its exact title); 'facts' are about that dish alone; 'topics' are the subjects whose facts it also draws on. Facts come up shuffled, each once before any comes round again. tools/facts_check.tscn counts them.

eggs: A fresh egg sinks in a bowl of water. An old one floats, because the air pocket inside grows as it ages.
The color of an eggshell comes from the breed of hen, not from how good the egg is.
Brown and white eggs taste the same and are just as good for you.
Hens with white earlobes mostly lay white eggs, and hens with red earlobes mostly lay brown ones.
Some hens, like the Araucana, lay blue eggs.
A hen takes about a day to make one egg.
An eggshell has thousands of tiny pores that let air in and out.
The cloudier a raw egg white is, the fresher the egg.
Those white strings in an egg are called chalazae. They hold the yolk in the middle, and fresh eggs have stronger ones.
Egg whites whip best at room temperature.
Even a drop of yolk can stop egg whites from whipping up, because fat breaks down the foam.
Whipped egg whites can grow to about eight times the size they started.
A pinch of cream of tartar helps whipped egg whites hold their shape.
A copper bowl helps egg whites whip into a steadier foam: a little copper bonds with the egg's proteins.
Egg whites start to set at a lower heat than yolks do.
Spin an egg to see if it's cooked: a hard-boiled egg spins smoothly, and a raw one wobbles.
Older eggs are easier to peel after boiling than very fresh ones.
A green ring round a hard-boiled yolk means it cooked too long. It's harmless: iron from the yolk meeting sulfur from the white.
Cooling boiled eggs in ice water stops them cooking and makes them easier to peel.
Egg yolks get their color from what the hen eats. Marigold petals and corn make them brighter.
Mayonnaise works because egg yolk holds oil and water together.
The part of the yolk that holds oil and water together is called lecithin.
Custard thickens because heated egg proteins join up into a soft net.
Stir hot milk into eggs a little at a time, so they warm up slowly and don't scramble. Cooks call it tempering.
For creamy scrambled eggs, cook them slowly and take them off while they still look a little wet.
Salting eggs a few minutes before scrambling them helps keep them tender.
An ostrich egg holds about as much as two dozen hen's eggs.
Quail eggs are so small it takes about five to match one hen's egg.
A double-yolked egg happens when a hen releases two yolks close together, often when she's young.
Eggs are easiest to separate cold, straight from the fridge.
An egg is about three quarters water.
Store eggs with the pointy end down: it keeps the yolk centered and the air pocket at the top.
In many countries eggs sit out on the counter. In the US they're washed first, so they have to stay in the fridge.
Nearly all of an egg's fat is in the yolk.
A poached egg holds together best when it's very fresh.
A splash of vinegar in the water helps a poached egg's white set faster.
A hen turns her eggs many times a day while she sits on them.
A hen eats extra calcium to make shells, and some farmers feed them crushed oyster shell.
Egg wash, a beaten egg brushed on dough, is what gives pastries their shiny golden tops.
An egg wash with just yolk bakes darker, and one with just white bakes shinier and paler.
Meringue is nothing but egg whites and sugar, whipped full of air.
A soufflé rises because the air in its egg whites swells in the oven.
French chefs' tall hats are said to have a pleat for every way to cook an egg. It's a good story, though nobody can prove it.
Chicks breathe inside the egg through its tiny pores.
China raises more eggs than any other country.
flour: Wheat is grown on more land than any other food crop.
Flour and water make gluten, a stretchy net that traps air and makes bread chewy.
Bread flour has more protein than cake flour, so it makes a chewier dough.
Resting dough lets the gluten relax, so it rolls out without springing back.
Kneading lines up strands of gluten so the dough gets smooth and stretchy.
Dough is kneaded enough when you can stretch a bit so thin that light shows through. Bakers call it the windowpane test.
Yeast is alive. It eats sugars in the dough and gives off the gas that makes bread rise.
One gram of yeast holds billions of cells.
Water that's too hot kills yeast. It should feel about as warm as your wrist.
Dough rises more slowly in the fridge, but it ends up with more flavor.
Salt slows yeast down, which helps bread rise evenly.
People were baking flatbread over 14,000 years ago, long before anyone farmed.
Ancient Egyptians are thought to be the first to bake bread that rose.
Sourdough rises with wild yeast that lives in the flour and the air.
Some sourdough starters have been kept alive for over a hundred years.
Whole wheat flour includes the bran and the germ. White flour is only the starchy middle of the grain.
Whole wheat flour goes stale sooner, because the germ has oil in it.
Baking powder has a dry acid mixed in. Baking soda needs something sour in the batter to work.
Most baking powder bubbles twice: once when it gets wet, and again when it gets hot.
Flour dust hanging in the air can catch fire, so mills kept flames well away.
Sifting flour breaks up the lumps and lets air in.
A cup of flour can weigh very different amounts depending on how tightly it's packed, so bakers use scales.
The brown crust on bread comes from the Maillard reaction, where sugars and proteins brown in the heat.
A tap on the bottom of a baked loaf should sound hollow.
Steam in the oven keeps a loaf's skin soft at first, so it can rise higher.
Bread goes stale faster in the fridge than on the counter.
Stale bread can be freshened in a hot oven: the heat loosens its starch again.
A baker's dozen is thirteen. Bakers may have added one so nobody could say they'd been cheated.
The holes in bread are the shapes the gas bubbles left behind.
Corn, rice and oats have no gluten of their own.
Bread was once used as plates. Slabs of stale bread, called trenchers, soaked up the gravy.
Before erasers, people rubbed out pencil marks with bread.
Sliced bread was first sold in 1928, in Missouri.
A grain of wheat has three parts: bran outside, starch inside, and a tiny germ that would sprout.
Durum wheat is so hard it's ground into coarse yellow semolina for pasta.
Stone mills crush grain between two turning stones. Modern mills use steel rollers.
Cornstarch thickens sauces clear and shiny, while flour makes them cloudy.
To thicken a sauce with flour without lumps, cook it in butter first. That's called a roux.
Toasting flour in a dry pan gives it a nutty taste.
Raw flour isn't safe to eat: it hasn't been heated to kill germs.
Cover resting dough with a damp towel so it doesn't grow a dry skin.
Sweet doughs rise slowly, because sugar takes water away from the yeast.
Punching down dough pushes out big bubbles so the loaf has an even crumb.
Docking means poking holes in dough so steam can get out and it stays flat.
A little honey keeps bread soft for longer, because it holds on to water.
Some Roman loaves were stamped to show whose they were. One was found in Herculaneum, nearly 2,000 years old.
dairy: It takes about 21 pounds of milk to make a pound of butter.
Butter is mostly fat, with a little water mixed through it.
Water in butter turns to steam in the oven, and that steam puffs up pastry.
Browned butter smells like hazelnuts. The French call it beurre noisette.
Clarified butter has the milk solids taken out, so it can get hotter before it burns.
Ghee is butter cooked until its water is gone and its milk solids brown. It's loved in Indian kitchens.
Butter left out softens, but it shouldn't melt: once melted, it never goes back to quite the same.
Cold butter makes flaky pastry. Soft butter makes fluffy cakes.
Creaming butter and sugar beats in tiny air bubbles that help cakes rise.
Whip cream too long and it turns into butter.
Cold cream in a cold bowl whips faster.
Milk looks white because tiny drops of fat and protein scatter light every way.
Cows have one stomach with four parts.
A dairy cow drinks enough water in a day to fill a small bathtub.
Homogenized milk is squeezed through tiny holes so its cream can't float to the top.
Pasteurizing, warming milk to kill germs, is named after Louis Pasteur.
Stir milk as it heats, or a skin forms on top and its bottom scorches.
Buttermilk was once what was left over from churning butter.
A spoonful of lemon juice in milk curdles it into a stand-in for buttermilk.
Yogurt is milk thickened by friendly bacteria that turn its sugar sour.
Ice cream stays soft partly because air is whipped into it.
A Holstein cow's spots are like fingerprints: no two are the same.
Butter churning is thousands of years old.
Cream rises because fat is lighter than the rest of the milk.
Condensed milk is milk with more than half its water boiled away, and lots of sugar.
Goat's milk has smaller drops of fat than cow's milk, so its cream takes longer to rise.
Water buffalo milk is so rich it's used to make the creamiest mozzarella.
Horses, camels, yaks and reindeer are all milked somewhere in the world.
Butter gets its yellow from the grass cows eat, so summer butter is often deeper yellow.
Salted butter was first made to keep longer.
Butter soaks up smells, so keep it wrapped in the fridge.
To soften butter quickly, cut it into small cubes.
Butter starts melting near body temperature, which is why it melts on your tongue.
Sour cream curdles if it boils, so stir it into hot food at the end.
Cream with more fat is less likely to curdle in a sauce.
Béchamel, a sauce of butter, flour and milk, is one of the five French mother sauces.
Butter sculptures have been a show at American state fairs for over a hundred years.
Bog butter, buried hundreds of years ago, still turns up in Ireland's peat bogs.
A pat of butter stirred into a sauce at the end makes it glossy.
sugar: Sugar was once so rare in Europe it was kept locked in boxes and sold by apothecaries.
Table sugar comes from two very different plants: sugarcane, a grass, and sugar beets, a root.
Brown sugar is white sugar with molasses in it.
Brown sugar goes hard when its water dries out. A slice of bread in the jar softens it again.
Caramel is sugar cooked until it breaks apart into hundreds of new flavors.
Candy makers test hot sugar by dropping it in cold water: soft ball, hard ball, soft crack, hard crack.
Sugar does more than sweeten. It keeps cakes soft by holding on to water.
A drop of lemon juice stops a sugar syrup from turning to crystals.
Cotton candy was made popular by a dentist, William Morrison, in 1897.
It takes about 40 gallons of maple sap to make one gallon of syrup.
Maple sap runs best when nights freeze and days thaw.
Maple sap looks and tastes almost like water. Boiling is what makes it syrup.
Quebec makes most of the world's maple syrup.
Quebec keeps a huge reserve of maple syrup in barrels, and in 2012 thieves got away with thousands of tons.
Darker maple syrup is made later in the season and tastes stronger.
A honeybee makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life.
Bees visit around two million flowers to make a pound of honey.
Bees fan honey with their wings to dry it out.
Honey's flavor changes with the flowers: orange blossom, clover and heather all taste different.
Honey gone grainy isn't spoiled. Warm the jar gently and it turns runny again.
Bees tell each other where flowers are by dancing.
Honeycomb cells are six-sided, a shape that holds the most honey with the least wax.
Powdered sugar usually has a little cornstarch in it, to stop it clumping.
Sugar crystals sparkle because each one has flat sides like a tiny gem.
Rock candy is grown: crystals gather on a string hung in sugar water.
Adding sugar to strawberries draws out their juice and makes a syrup.
Jam keeps well because sugar ties up the water germs would need.
Marshmallows were first made from a real plant, the marsh mallow, which grows in marshes.
Sugar raises the boiling point of water, so syrup gets much hotter than soup. Be careful!
A pinch of salt makes sweet things taste sweeter.
Cinnamon is the inside bark of a tree. It curls up as it dries.
Vanilla comes from an orchid, and each flower opens for only a day.
Nearly all vanilla flowers are pollinated by hand.
Vanilla is one of the most expensive spices in the world, after saffron.
Nutmeg and mace come from the same fruit.
salt: Salt doesn't just make food salty. It wakes up other flavors and hides bitter ones.
Roman soldiers may have been paid partly in salt: the word salary comes from the Latin for salt.
Salt food from high up, so it falls evenly.
Kosher salt has big flakes that are easy to pinch.
A spoon of fine salt is much saltier than a spoon of flaky salt, because it packs closer together.
All salt came from the sea once, even salt that's mined from under mountains.
Salt draws water out of food. That's how pickles and hams are made.
Iodine is added to a lot of table salt to keep people healthy.
Pink Himalayan salt gets its color from traces of iron.
Cities grew up round salt mines. Salzburg means salt fortress.
There's a church carved out of salt deep in the Wieliczka mine in Poland.
Salt on an icy sidewalk melts ice because salty water freezes at a lower temperature.
If soup's too salty, add more unsalted water or broth. A potato won't soak up only the salt.
Acid can do some of the same work as salt: a squeeze of lemon wakes up a flat soup.
Pepper starts losing its smell as soon as it's ground, so grind it fresh.
Black, white and green peppercorns all grow on the same vine.
Pepper was once so valuable that people paid rent with it.
Pink peppercorns aren't really pepper at all.
Dried herbs go in early so they soften. Fresh tender herbs go in at the end.
Dried herbs are stronger than fresh ones, so use about a third as much.
Rub dried herbs between your fingers to wake up their smell.
Cooks tie herbs in a bundle called a bouquet garni so it's easy to fish out.
Bay leaves stay stiff however long they cook, so take them out before serving.
Saffron is the threads from crocus flowers. It takes tens of thousands of flowers to make a pound.
Basil bruises easily, so tear it or cut it with a very sharp knife.
Cilantro tastes like soap to some people, and it's partly in their genes.
Cilantro and coriander seed come from the same plant.
Oregano tastes stronger dried than fresh.
Mint spreads so fast that gardeners grow it in pots.
Rosemary means dew of the sea.
Thyme leaves are so small most cooks pull them off the stem backward with their fingers.
Garlic gets stronger the finer you chop it.
Garlic turns bitter when it burns, so add it after the onions.
Crushed garlic left to sit for a few minutes before cooking builds more flavor.
Umami, the savory fifth taste, was named by a Japanese scientist in 1908.
Mushrooms, tomatoes, seaweed and aged cheese are all full of umami.
Toasting whole spices in a dry pan brings out their oils.
Spices were one of the reasons explorers first sailed round the world.
Sea salt flakes are gathered from the top of drying ponds by hand.
cheese: There are more than a thousand kinds of cheese.
It takes about ten pounds of milk to make one pound of hard cheese.
Swiss cheese's holes are called eyes, and they're made by gas bubbles.
Cheddar gets its name from a village in England.
Orange cheddar is colored with annatto, a seed from a tropical tree.
Parmesan is aged for at least a year, and often for two or three.
A whole wheel of Parmigiano Reggiano weighs about 80 pounds.
There are banks in Italy that take wheels of Parmesan as security for loans.
Mozzarella is stretched in hot water until it's smooth and stringy.
Cheese is easier to grate when it's cold.
Young cheeses melt best. Aged ones, like Parmesan, go grainy on their own.
Cheese splits when it's too hot: the fat leaks out of its proteins.
A little starch keeps cheese sauce smooth, because it stops the proteins from clumping.
Rennet, which sets milk into curd, traditionally comes from a calf's stomach.
The liquid left after making cheese is called whey.
Ricotta means recooked: it's made by cooking the whey again.
Halloumi from Cyprus can be grilled without melting.
Blue cheese gets its veins from friendly mold. Cheese makers poke holes to let air in so it can grow.
Roquefort is aged in caves in the south of France.
Crystals in old cheese that crunch are made of amino acids. They're a sign of age.
Gouda is pronounced more like HOW-da in Dutch.
Feta is kept in salty water.
Brie and Camembert ripen from the outside in.
Let cheese warm up before you eat it: cold hides its flavor.
Wrap cheese in paper, not just plastic, so it can breathe.
Cheese may have been discovered by accident, when milk was carried in a pouch made from a stomach.
Pieces of strainers with traces of cheese on them have been found from more than 7,000 years ago.
The world's oldest cheese so far was found in a tomb in China.
Every year people chase a wheel of cheese down a steep hill in Gloucestershire, England.
Somebody who loves cheese is called a turophile.
Cheese from different seasons tastes different, because cows eat different plants.
Cheddaring is stacking slabs of curd on top of each other to press out the whey.
Cheese curds squeak when they're fresh.
Wisconsin makes more cheese than any other US state.
Monterey Jack was first made in California.
Colby is named after a town in Wisconsin.
Pecorino is made from sheep's milk: pecora means sheep in Italian.
Gruyère gets nutty and sweet as it ages, which is why it's loved in fondue.
Fondue means melted in French.
Grating cheese gives it more surface, so it melts quickly and evenly.
Provolone is hung from ropes to age.
Washed-rind cheeses smell much stronger than they taste.
The rind of a hard cheese can be simmered in soup for flavor.
pasta: There are more than 300 shapes of pasta.
Farfalle means butterflies in Italian.
Vermicelli means little worms.
Orecchiette means little ears.
Linguine means little tongues.
Penne means quills, after the pens they look like.
Conchiglie means shells.
Salt pasta water well: it's the only chance to season the pasta itself.
Oil in the water doesn't stop pasta sticking. Stirring in the first minute does.
Finish pasta in its sauce so they soak each other up.
Don't rinse hot pasta for a sauce. The starch helps the sauce stick.
Ridges on pasta hold on to sauce.
Thick, chunky sauces go with big shapes, and thin ones go with long strands.
Pasta dough of flour and water can be dried for years. Fresh egg pasta cooks in a couple of minutes.
Bronze dies make pasta with a rough surface that sauce loves.
Italians eat more pasta per person than anybody else.
In 1957, British TV fooled people on April Fools' Day with a film of spaghetti growing on trees.
Noodles about 4,000 years old were found in a bowl in China.
Marco Polo didn't bring pasta to Italy. It was already there.
Pulled noodles are stretched and folded again and again by hand until there are hundreds.
Ramen noodles get their spring and yellow color from alkaline mineral water.
Instant noodles were invented in Japan in 1958 by Momofuku Ando.
Instant noodles are dried by frying, which leaves tiny holes that soak up hot water.
Soba noodles are made from buckwheat, which isn't a kind of wheat.
Udon are thick and chewy, and the dough is sometimes kneaded by foot.
Slurping noodles is good manners in Japan. It cools them and brings out the smell.
Long noodles stand for a long life, so they're eaten on birthdays in China.
Rice noodles can be soaked instead of boiled.
Glass noodles go clear when they're cooked. They're made from mung bean or sweet potato starch.
Some instant noodles have even been to space.
There's a Cup Noodles museum in Yokohama where you can design your own cup.
Thomas Jefferson loved macaroni so much he drew a plan of a pasta machine.
A macaroni pie was served at a White House dinner in 1802.
Pasta puffs up by about double as it cooks.
A pot boils over because starch makes the bubbles strong. A wooden spoon across the top helps pop them.
Pasta water should boil hard, so the pasta keeps moving and doesn't clump.
Egg noodles are richer and softer than plain ones.
Tossing noodles with a little sauce right away keeps them from sticking together.
rice: Rice feeds more than half the people in the world.
There are tens of thousands of kinds of rice.
Rice grows in flooded fields called paddies. The water keeps weeds away.
Sushi rice is sticky because it has more of a starch called amylopectin.
Basmati means fragrant.
Rinsing rice washes off loose starch so the grains don't clump.
Let rice rest with the lid on after cooking, so its steam evens out.
Don't stir rice while it cooks, unless you want it sticky like risotto.
Risotto is stirred on purpose: rubbing the grains together makes it creamy.
Leftover cold rice makes the best fried rice, because it's drier.
Rice almost triples in size when it's cooked.
Brown rice is white rice with its bran still on.
Wild rice isn't really rice. It's the seed of a different water grass.
In Japanese, the word for cooked rice also means meal.
People have grown rice for around 9,000 years.
Terraced rice paddies in the Philippines have been farmed for hundreds of years.
In some countries ducks are let into rice paddies to eat the bugs and weeds.
Rice is thrown at weddings to wish the couple plenty.
Crispy rice from the bottom of the pot is a treat all over the world. Persians call it tahdig.
Koreans call the crispy rice at the bottom of the pot nurungji.
Socarrat is the crispy layer at the bottom of a paella.
The Great Wall of China has sticky rice in its mortar, which made it stronger.
Electric rice cookers know the rice is done when the water's gone and it starts to heat up past boiling.
Rice flour makes batter extra crisp, because it has no gluten.
Puffed rice pops because the water inside turns to steam.
Black rice was once called forbidden rice.
Sushi was first a way of keeping fish: it was packed in rice that went sour.
Season sushi rice while it's hot, fanning it so it turns glossy.
Onigiri are rice balls, and people in Japan have been eating them for over a thousand years.
There's a kind of rice that smells like popcorn: it has the same scent molecule.
Some rice grows in deep floods: it can shoot up inches in a day to stay above the water.
Rice straw is woven into rope, mats and sandals.
tomato: Tomatoes are a fruit, and a berry at that.
A US court ruled in 1893 that tomatoes should be taxed as vegetables.
Tomatoes came from the Americas. Italians didn't use them much until the 1700s.
People in Europe once thought tomatoes were poisonous, because they're related to nightshade.
Don't keep tomatoes in the fridge: the cold dulls their flavor.
Cooking tomatoes makes their red color, lycopene, easier for your body to use.
A pinch of sugar balances sour tomatoes.
To peel tomatoes, dip them in boiling water for a few seconds and then in ice water.
Ketchup started in Southeast Asia as a sauce made from fermented fish.
Early English ketchups were made from mushrooms, walnuts and even oysters.
Tomato ketchup wasn't written down until 1812.
Ketchup is stuck until you push it hard enough, then it flows all at once. Scientists call it shear thinning.
Tap the neck of a glass ketchup bottle, not its bottom, to get it going.
Ketchup is sweet, sour, salty, savory and a little bitter all at once.
Green ketchup was sold in 2000, and lots of kids loved it.
Heirloom tomatoes come in purple, yellow, green and stripes.
There are more than 10,000 kinds of tomato.
The biggest tomato ever grown weighed over ten pounds.
A tomato plant's smell comes mostly from its leaves and stem.
Every summer in Buñol, Spain, thousands of people throw tomatoes at each other.
Tomato seeds have grown after years in space.
Tomato paste is tomatoes cooked down until they're thick. Frying it makes it sweeter.
San Marzano tomatoes grow near Mount Vesuvius in soil from the volcano.
Tomatoes ripen faster in a paper bag with a banana, because bananas give off a ripening gas.
Tomato plants tell each other about bugs through scents in the air.
Bumblebees shake tomato flowers with their buzz to get the pollen out.
Cherry tomatoes are closer to wild tomatoes than big ones are.
Salt a sliced tomato a few minutes before eating it to bring out its juice.
Add basil to tomato sauce at the end, so it stays fresh.
A wooden spoon stained orange by tomato sauce comes clean in the sun.
chili: Chili peppers feel hot because of capsaicin, which tricks your nerves into feeling a burn.
Birds can't feel the heat of chilies, so they spread the seeds.
A chili's heat is measured in Scoville units, named after Wilbur Scoville.
Scoville first measured heat by watering down chili until tasters couldn't feel it anymore.
A bell pepper scores zero on the Scoville scale.
A jalapeño is usually between 2,500 and 8,000 Scoville units.
Pepper X holds the record for the hottest chili, at over two million Scoville units.
The hottest part of a chili is the white part that holds the seeds, not the seeds themselves.
Wash your hands after cutting chilies, and don't rub your eyes!
Chilies came from the Americas, so there was no chili in Asia until about 500 years ago.
People have grown chilies in Mexico for more than 6,000 years.
A red chili is usually a green one that's been left to ripen.
Dried chilies have new names: a dried jalapeño, smoked, is a chipotle.
A dried poblano is called an ancho.
Paprika is ground from dried red peppers.
Sichuan peppercorns make your mouth tingle, as if it were buzzing.
Sichuan peppercorns aren't related to chilies or black pepper. They're in the citrus family.
Scientists found the tingle of Sichuan pepper feels like a vibration 50 times a second.
Kimchi is cabbage fermented with chili, garlic and ginger.
Koreans have been eating chili in kimchi for a few hundred years.
Gochujang is a Korean paste of chili, rice and fermented soybeans.
Chili oil's flavor comes out in warm oil, not hot: too hot and it burns.
Eating chilies makes you sweat, which helps cool you down in hot places.
Some farmers grow chilies round their crops to keep elephants away.
Ginger and turmeric are underground stems, not roots.
Wasabi's heat goes up your nose because it's a gas, and it fades in seconds.
Most wasabi outside Japan is really horseradish, colored green.
Mustard has no heat until its seeds are crushed and wet.
Adding a little sugar or fat calms down a dish that's too spicy.
People get used to chili. The more you eat, the less it burns.
The word chili comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs.
Frying chilies makes the whole kitchen cough. Open a window!
pork: Bacon is pork belly that's been cured with salt, and often smoked.
Start bacon in a cold pan: its fat melts slowly and it cooks more evenly.
Canadian bacon comes from the loin, so it's much leaner.
In Britain, bacon is usually cut from the back.
Bacon smells so good because its sugars and proteins make hundreds of scents as it browns.
Save bacon fat in a jar: it's great for frying potatoes or eggs.
Pancetta is like bacon but it's cured without smoke.
Prosciutto takes a year or more to dry.
Pigs are clever. They can learn to play simple video games with a joystick.
Pigs can't sweat much, so they roll in mud to keep cool.
Pigs have a sense of smell good enough to find truffles under the ground.
Pork is the most eaten meat in much of East Asia.
Curing salt is what keeps bacon and ham pink.
Let pork rest after cooking so the juices settle back in.
Pork can be served a little pink in the middle: 145°F with a rest is safe for whole cuts.
Ground pork should be cooked all the way through.
Mix ground pork in one direction so it gets sticky and springy. That's the trick to juicy dumplings.
A spoonful of water or stock stirred into ground pork keeps dumplings juicy.
Ginger and scallions are put in pork dumplings to balance the rich meat.
Lard makes very flaky pie crust, because its crystals are large.
Sausages are some of the oldest prepared foods. There's one mentioned in the Odyssey.
Frankfurters are named after Frankfurt, and wieners after Vienna.
Char siu means fork roasted: strips of pork were hung on forks over the fire.
Pulled pork gets tender because its tough collagen slowly melts into gelatin.
A pig's nose has a disc of cartilage that helps it dig.
Wild boar are the ancestors of farm pigs.
Black pepper and pork are friends all over the world.
Ham is the back leg, and shoulder is the front.
Bacon strips cook flatter between two baking trays in the oven.
A little water in the pan with bacon keeps the fat from spitting at first.
beef: The crust on a steak is the Maillard reaction, named after the French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard.
Cut steak across the grain, so the fibers are short and it's tender.
Salt a steak either just before cooking or at least 40 minutes before.
Marbling is the little lines of fat in beef. They melt and keep it juicy.
Wagyu means Japanese cow.
Fat carries flavor, so a well-marbled steak tastes richer.
Turning a steak often makes it cook more evenly and a little faster.
A thermometer is the surest way to know a steak is done.
A rare steak is about 125°F inside, and a medium one is about 140°F.
Steak keeps cooking after it's off the heat. Take it off a few degrees early.
The red juice in a steak isn't blood. It's water with a protein called myoglobin.
Muscles a cow uses a lot, like its legs, are tougher but full of flavor.
The tenderloin hardly does any work, so it's the softest cut.
A T-bone has two cuts in one: strip on one side, tenderloin on the other.
Dry-aged beef loses water and gets nuttier as it hangs.
Cast iron holds its heat, so it doesn't cool when a steak lands on it.
Listen to your pan: a loud sizzle means it's hot enough.
Baste a steak with butter and herbs at the end, so the butter doesn't burn.
Leave some space between steaks. Crowding a pan traps steam.
A steak from the fridge sears fine, but it takes longer to warm inside.
Ground beef has more surface than a steak, so it needs to be cooked all the way through.
Press a burger only once and only early, or you squeeze out its juice.

Fish often bite best around dawn and dusk, when the light is low and lots of insects are out.
Wash the cleanest things first, like glasses, then plates, then greasy pans, so the water stays cleaner for longer.
Pat steak dry before searing: a wet surface steams instead of browning.
The brown crust on a seared steak is the Maillard reaction: proteins and sugars browning at around 140 °C (285 °F) and up.
Searing doesn't really seal in a steak's juices. What it adds is flavor, from all that browning.
Let a steak rest for a few minutes after cooking, so its juices settle before you cut it.
